5922: Accused of blasphemy for claiming to be God's Son, Jesus quotes Ps 82:6, "I said, you are gods", and argues from lesser to greater: if Scripture called others "gods", how can it be blasphemy for the one the Father consecrated and sent to say "I am the Son of God"? Council readers think Jesus refers to the divine beings of Ps 82, and that his point is that Scripture already knows of plural elohim and of a Son with a unique role; the phrase "to whom the word of God came" refers to the beings God addressed in the psalm.
5923: Many commentators think Jesus means human judges or leaders who received God's word, so his argument is: even humans can be called "gods" in Scripture, so the title alone is no blasphemy. Others (e.g. Jerome Neyrey) argue for the rabbinic reading that the psalm addresses Israel at Sinai, who received God's word (the law). All agree the argument is not that Jesus is merely one god among many; John's Gospel presents him as uniquely one with the Father (John 10:30; John 1:1).
5924: Are demons the spirits of the dead Nephilim?
5925: This idea is stated in 1 Enoch 15:8-12: when the giants died, evil spirits came out of their bodies and roam the earth. It was widely believed in Second Temple Judaism and by some early Christian writers (e.g. Justin Martyr, Athenagoras). Heiser and others suggest it may explain why demons in the Gospels seek bodies to inhabit (Matt 12:43-45) and why they are distinguished from fallen angels kept in chains (Jude 1:6). It should be labelled clearly: the Bible itself never says where demons come from.
5926: The dominant Christian view (Augustine, Aquinas, the Reformers, most theologians today) is that demons are fallen angels who followed Satan (based on Matt 25:41; Rev 12:7-9). Others treat the Bible's language about demons as reflecting the world-view of its time without settling their origin, and some scholars see the Enochic story as a way Jewish writers explained the origin of evil without blaming humans alone. The Old Testament's "demons" (shedim, Deut 32:17; Ps 106:37) are identified with the gods of the nations, not with Nephilim.
5927: Did Israel's religion evolve from polytheism?
5928: Council readers argue that the Bible's council is not a leftover from polytheism but a deliberate part of its theology, carried into the New Testament (Eph 6:12; Col 1:16). They accept that many Israelites worshipped other gods (the Bible says so constantly), but distinguish what the people did from what the biblical writers taught. They also note that Yahweh is presented as unique even in old poetry such as Exod 15:11 ("Who is like you among the gods?").
5929: Many historians (Mark Smith, Rainer Albertz and others) argue that early Israelite religion included El, Yahweh, Baal and Asherah; that Yahweh absorbed El's roles and titles; and that strict monotheism emerged late, around the exile. Evidence includes inscriptions such as "Yahweh and his asherah" at Kuntillet Ajrud, the prophets' own complaints (Jer 11:13), and Josiah's reforms (2 Kgs 23:4-14). Yehezkel Kaufmann, by contrast, argued Israel's religion was monotheistic from the start and that popular idolatry was a corruption. Many scholars today take a middle position: official Yahweh-only worship coexisted with widespread folk religion, and the writers' convictions sharpened over time.
5930: If idols are "nothing", how can the gods be real?
5931: Paul holds both together: "an idol has no real existence" and "there is no God but one" (1 Cor 8:4), yet "what pagans sacrifice they offer to demons and not to God" (1 Cor 10:20). He is echoing Deut 32:17, which calls the nations' gods shedim (demons) and "not God". Council readers see a consistent picture: the statue is just wood or stone, but real spiritual powers can stand behind the cult; they are "by nature not gods" (Gal 4:8) in the full sense, because only the Creator is God.
5932: Some interpreters read Paul's "demons" as a way of saying idolatry is spiritually destructive rather than as a claim about beings behind each idol, and read the Old Testament's mockery of idols (Isa 44; Jer 10:3-5) as denying any reality to the gods at all. Classical theology generally accepted that demons can exploit idol worship while insisting the "gods" as such are false.
5934: "The Council of Yahweh", *Journal of Theological Studies* 45
5935: An early, influential article arguing that the Old Testament pictures Yahweh surrounded by a heavenly court, and that the prophets claimed to have stood in it (Jer 23:18, 22). It put the council on the agenda of modern Old Testament study.
5938: Compared Ugaritic myths about El, his assembly and Baal with Israel's poetry and prophecy, arguing that Yahweh took over many of El's features and that the prophet was a messenger of the divine council. Shaped a generation of Harvard-trained scholars.
5940: "Cosmology and World Order in the Old Testament: The Divine Council as Cosmic-Political Symbol"; earlier *The Divine Warrior in Early Israel* (1973)
5941: Showed how the council works in the Old Testament as a picture of God's government of the world, linking heavenly decisions to justice on earth (as in Ps 82), and traced the heavenly host as Yahweh's army.
5943: *The Assembly of the Gods: The Divine Council in Canaanite and Early Hebrew Literature*
5944: The first full-length study comparing the council of El at Ugarit with the council of Yahweh in the Hebrew Bible, covering its members, meeting places and functions.
5946: *The Origins of Biblical Monotheism*; also *The Early History of God* (1990, 2nd ed. 2002)
5947: Argues that Israel's religion developed from a family-style pantheon (El, his sons, Yahweh, Baal, Asherah) to monolatry and finally to explicit monotheism around the exile, with the council texts as traces of the earlier stages. The leading evolutionary account, widely respected but disputed by more traditional scholars.
5949: *The Unseen Realm*; doctoral dissertation (University of Wisconsin–Madison, 2004) on the divine council in late canonical and Second Temple Jewish literature
5950: Synthesised the council material into a whole-Bible theology for a popular evangelical audience: the three rebellions, the Deut 32 "cosmic geography" of nations under lesser gods, and the New Testament as the reclaiming of the nations. Very influential at the popular level; critics say it builds a large system on a few texts and sometimes treats possible readings as settled.
5952: "Of Demigods and the Deluge: Toward an Interpretation of Genesis 6:1-4", *Journal of Biblical Literature* 106
5953: Argued that Gen 6:1-4 is a short myth of divine beings mating with women, related to ancient Near Eastern and Greek stories of demigods, and that the flood answers the blurring of the boundary between gods and humans.
5955: *One God, One Lord: Early Christian Devotion and Ancient Jewish Monotheism*; later *Lord Jesus Christ* (2003)
5956: Showed that Second Temple Judaism, while speaking of many angelic beings and exalted figures, reserved worship for God alone, and that the earliest Christians strikingly included Jesus in that worship. Key for seeing where Jesus fits relative to the council.
5957: *Jesus and the God of Israel* (expanding *God Crucified*, 1998)
5958: Argues that Jewish monotheism was defined by God's unique identity (sole Creator and sole Ruler over all, to whom alone worship is due) and that the New Testament places Jesus within that identity, not among the angels or council members. A strong counterweight to readings that make Christ one exalted being among many.
5961: Questions models that divide the council into fixed tiers borrowed from Ugarit (such as Lowell Handy's four-level pantheon), arguing that the biblical texts show a looser and more varied picture. Her work is a useful check on neat "three-tier" schemes, including popular ones.
